Numeric date order of this system
nodes.instructions:
You read one paragraph of source notes (input block "paragraph") that describes a legacy system (named in "system"). Decide how this system writes NUMERIC dates such as 07/05/1962: day first ("dmy") or month first ("mdy"). For VENDEX the question covers all its numeric dates; for BRIGHTDESK and ATLAS it covers numeric birth dates.
Return:
- basis: how the paragraph settles it:
  "explicit" = it states the order itself (day first / month first, DD/MM/YYYY / MM/DD/YYYY, UK or US locale, European or American convention, including negated forms such as "never writes the month first");
  "example" = it gives an example numeric date and says what it means (a full date, or only the month someone was born in / a date falls in);
  "same_as_system" = it says the order is the same as another system's;
  "place" = it gives only a place (the city the team works in now, or the country where the servers stand) and says dates are written the way people there do.
- order: your reading, "dmy" or "mdy".
- quote: the one sentence that settles it, copied exactly, character for character, from the paragraph.
- example_numeric / example_meaning: for basis "example", the example numeric date exactly as written (e.g. "06/11/1964") and the words that say what it means exactly as written (e.g. "6 November 1964" or "March"); otherwise null.
- same_as_system: for basis "same_as_system", the other system's name; otherwise "none".
- moved_from / place / place_in_united_states: for basis "place". If the text says the team moved ("moved from A to B"), moved_from is A, the place it moved FROM, exactly as written, and place is B, the place it moved TO and works in now; otherwise moved_from is null and place is the place given (where the team works, or the country where the servers stand), exactly as written. place_in_united_states says whether "place" (B, not A) is in the United States. All three are null for other bases.
If the paragraph also says the order changed at some date (a vendor move), answer for the order BEFORE that change (the original order, not the one that applies afterwards). Ignore sentences about other kinds of dates (update dates, era dates, ISO dates).

nodes.instructions:
You read the source-notes paragraph of the ATLAS ledger (input block "paragraph"). Some ATLAS installations changed how they write numeric birth dates on a given day (for example when the hosting vendor changed): rows last changed on or after that day use a different order. Decide whether this paragraph describes such a dated change.
Return:
- present: true only if the paragraph says numeric birth dates are written differently in rows changed on/after a certain date.
- quote: that sentence copied exactly, character for character (null if not present).
- switch_date: the date of the change exactly as written in that sentence, e.g. "19 April 2023" (null if not present). Other dates in the paragraph (for example the date ATLAS went live) are not the change date.
- after: how numeric birth dates are written in rows changed on/after the change: "swapped" (day and month the other way round from before), "day_first" or "month_first"; "none" if not present.
- boundary: "on_or_after" if rows changed ON that day already use the new order, "after" if only rows changed strictly later do; "none" if not present.

nodes.description: Meaning of this status value
nodes.instructions:
You read the source-notes paragraph of one legacy system (input block "paragraph") and one status value ("token") that occurs in that system's rows. Decide what the notes say about rows carrying this value: "void" (not a real account: excluded from the migration, dropped, left out) or "live" (a real account: kept and migrated). Labels can be misleading; only what the notes say counts.
Return:
- meaning: "void" or "live".
- relation / compared_with: if the notes define the value by comparison with one of the system's fixed markers, give the relation and that marker:
  relation "same_as" for "treat rows marked X exactly like Y" (X means the same as Y);
  relation "different_from" for "do not confuse X with Y" (X is NOT like Y);
  compared_with is Y, one of: "stage=customer", "ZZTEST", "aktiv", "gesperrt", "storniert", "DO NOT MIGRATE", "SAMPLE", "sandbox", "production", or "ordinary_live_rows" (ordinary member/customer rows). Otherwise relation "none" and compared_with "none".
- quote: the sentence about this value copied exactly, character for character, from the paragraph.
Fixed meanings for reference: stage=customer, aktiv, gesperrt and production are live; ZZTEST, storniert, DO NOT MIGRATE, SAMPLE and sandbox are void.

nodes.instructions:
You read the source-notes paragraph of one legacy system (input block "paragraph"; the system is named in "system"). Each row has an update date (updated / Geändert / ts). Decide whether the paragraph says this system's update dates are real change dates or not:
- "restamped": the dates are NOT real change dates; a copy job, mirror rebuild, restore from backup, migration to new hardware or re-import rewrote them (so they show copy/restore times).
- "real": the paragraph says the dates are real change dates (including "was rebuilt once but the rebuild kept the original dates", or "this system writes its own dates and is not a copy").
- "not_stated": the paragraph says nothing about whether its update dates are reliable.
Return update_dates and quote: the sentence that settles it, copied exactly, character for character (null for not_stated).

Which side this system prints balances from
nodes.instructions:
You read the source-notes paragraph of one legacy system (input block "paragraph"; the system is named in "system"). Its rows print a balance (balance / Saldo / owed). The canonical master stores money the account holder owes US as a positive number and money WE owe them (a credit they hold with us) as a negative number. Decide what happens to a POSITIVE printed balance of this system in the master:
- positive_in_master: "positive" if the master keeps a positive printed figure positive (the printed figure is what they owe us: a receivable, an open invoice, unpaid orders, read literally); "negative" if it becomes negative (the printed figure is what we owe them: a credit, prepaid deposit, store credit, a payable; or the notes say the balances change sign / are printed the opposite way / must be flipped for the master).
- positive_printed_balance_means: "they_owe_us" (goes with "positive") or "we_owe_them" (goes with "negative"). A paragraph that only says the sign changes in the master means a positive printed figure is money we owe them.
- negative_printed_balance_means: what a NEGATIVE printed figure (one marked with a minus, parentheses, "CR" or "▲") means according to the paragraph: "they_owe_us" or "we_owe_them".
- master_span: the words of the paragraph that say what the MASTER does with this system's balances, copied exactly (for example a phrase saying the balance is negative or positive in the master, keeps its sign, changes sign, is flipped, is recorded with the opposite sign, or is printed the same way as the master); null if the paragraph says nothing about the master.
- quote: the sentence that settles it, copied exactly, character for character, from the paragraph.
Read the positive and the negative case separately: a sentence may describe the positive figure first and then say how negative figures are marked.

VENDEX. Free-text English entries ("Vendex <id> — ...") written by the procurement team; the phrasing varies from entry to entry. Names are written given name first (with an optional title and middle initial). Dates — birth dates and the date the entry was revised — are written out in words or, when the day is 12 or less, sometimes numerically. The team moved from Houston to London in 2015 and has written numeric dates the local way ever since. A two-digit year in a birth date means 19xx. For a call note ("Spoke with <name> on <date>") the call date is the revision date. Balances may be written in words: "dollars" are US dollars, "euros" EUR and "pounds" GBP (pence are hundredths of a pound). "Owes us", "open balance", "outstanding" and "balance due" introduce what the supplier owes us; "in credit by", "holding a credit of", "credit balance of" and "we owe them" introduce a credit, that is a negative balance. An entry that ends with "(Application withdrawn — never onboarded.)" is void.

SOURCE NOTES — legacy systems in this export

The export merges 6 systems: BRIGHTDESK (US sales CRM), LEDGR (German ERP for customers and suppliers across Europe and beyond), ATLAS (UK supplier ledger), VENDEX (procurement team's free-text contact register), KOBO (Japanese web shop), VERITAS (identity-verification service for KYC checks). General: a blank field means the value is missing. So do the placeholders "n/a", "—", "TBD", "?", "00/00/0000", "00.00.0000", "----/--/--" and all-zero phone numbers. statusItems.paragraph: ATLAS. Lines look like "ATLAS #<id> :: <name> :: born <birth date> :: <country> :: tel <phone> :: owed <amount in GBP> :: last change <date>", optionally with ":: note: ..." and a trailing status tag (":: <TAG>"). Names are "FAMILY, Given (Title)" or "Title Given Family". Birth dates are written numerically or, when the day is above 12, with an abbreviated month name ("25 Mar 1985" or "25-Mar-1985"). Numeric birth dates in ATLAS use the same order as LEDGR (only the separator may differ). Since its migration to a new vendor on 8 November 2022, ATLAS has written numeric birth dates month first (month/day/year) in every row whose last change falls on or after that day; rows last changed earlier keep the order described above. Unknown birth dates appear as "n/k" or "?". "CR" after an amount marks a negative "owed" figure. Do not read "owed" literally: it is the amount we still have to pay the supplier, so flip its sign for the master. A line ending ":: DO NOT MIGRATE" is void. Rows marked ":: ARCHIVE" look like test data but are genuine, merely dormant accounts; they are not void.

VERITAS. Each line is "VERITAS " followed by a JSON object: row, family, given, dob (ISO date), country (ISO alpha-2, except that the United Kingdom is sometimes written "UK"; letter case varies), msisdn (the full international number including country code, without "+"), amount and ccy (ISO currency code), ts (time of last update, ISO 8601 UTC) and an optional note. A dob of 1900-01-01 is the vendor's sentinel for "unknown" and is not a real birth date. Rows containing "env":"sandbox" are test traffic and void. "env":"production" marks live traffic. Finance still invoices rows marked "env":"replay", so they are not void.

BRIGHTDESK. Lines look like "BRIGHTDESK row=<id> | name=... | dob=... | country=... | phone=... | balance=... | updated=YYYY-MM-DD", sometimes followed by "| memo=...". Birth dates are written numerically (zero padding is inconsistent) or, when the day is above 12, with an abbreviated month name ("25 Mar 1985"). Although BRIGHTDESK is a US sales CRM, the instance was cloned from the London office and runs in UK locale: numeric birth dates are day/month/year. Names are written either "Given FAMILY" (family name in capital letters; a title may precede the given name and a middle initial may follow it) or "Family, Given" (a middle initial may follow). Balances are in US dollars; a balance in parentheses, or with a leading minus, is negative. Balances are open invoices, not prepaid deposits: the customer owes us. Some reps typed 011, the US international access code, in front of the country code of foreign numbers. Some rows also carry a "stage" field; "stage=customer" is an ordinary live account. QA fixtures are void: a row whose name begins with "ZZTEST" must not be migrated. A row marked stage=migrated counts as carrying a void marker; drop it. BRIGHTDESK's updated is the real date of the last change; the vendor confirmed this during the 2024 audit.
